title: Predict the output
idea: Read // and % lines carefully and predict exactly what prints — before running.

exercises.explanation: Three 4s make 12, which fits in 15. // keeps only the whole part: 3.
15 minus the 12 from three 4s leaves 3. So 15 % 4 is 3.
No whole 7 fits inside 4, so 4 // 7 is 0 full groups. A smaller number over a bigger one gives 0.
Since no whole 7 fits in 4, nothing is used and all 4 is left over. So 4 % 7 is 4.
Ten 10s make 100 exactly. 100 // 10 is 10, with a leftover of 0.
100 shares into 10s perfectly, so nothing is left. 100 % 10 is 0.

exercises.prompt:
What will these two lines show?

n = 29
print(n // 10)
print(n % 10)
exercises.explanation: 29 // 10 is 2 (the tens), and 29 % 10 is 9 (the ones). // and % can even pull apart the digits of a number!

exercises.prompt: For any number shared into 10s, % 10 gives its last digit.
exercises.explanation: The leftover after whole 10s is exactly the ones digit. 47 % 10 is 7, 83 % 10 is 3. A neat trick.

exercises.prompt: Match each line to its output.
exercises.explanation: 13 shares into 5s as 2 groups with 3 left. The other way, no whole 13 fits in 5, so 0 groups and all 5 left over.

exercises.prompt: Before running, you predict print(22 % 5) shows 2. Are you right?
options: Yes — four 5s make 20, and 2 is left
exercises.explanation: Four 5s make 20, and 22 minus 20 is 2. Your prediction was right! Predicting first is how good programmers work.
